'''Benedict Hyman Gross'''<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> (June 22, 1950 – December 19, 2025) was an American mathematician who was a professor at the [[University of California, San Diego]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.math.ucsd.edu/people/profiles/benedict-gross/|title= Benedict Gross|website=[[University of California, San Diego]] |access-date=January 27, 2026}}</ref> the George Vasmer Leverett Professor of Mathematics Emeritus at [[Harvard University]], and [[Dean (education)|Dean]] of [[Harvard College]].<ref name="cv">[http://www.math.harvard.edu/~gross/CV09.pdf Curriculum vitae] from Gross's web site at Harvard, retrieved April 21, 2010.</ref>

Gross is known for his work in [[number theory]], particularly the [[Gross–Zagier theorem]] on [[L-function]]s of [[elliptic curve]]s, and related topics in [[algebraic geometry]], [[automorphic form]]s, and [[representation theory]]. He received a [[MacArthur Fellows Program|MacArthur Fellowship]] in 1986 and a [[Cole Prize]] in 1987. He was a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], a fellow of the [[American Philosophical Society]], and an elected member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]].

==Life and career==
===Early life and education===
Benedict Hyman Gross was born on June 22, 1950, in [[South Orange, New Jersey]], to Joel and Terry Gross.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> His father, Joel Gross, was born in [[Jersey City]] to Austrian immigrants who had moved to the United States as children.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> Joel Gross was a lawyer in [[Newark, New Jersey|Newark]] and was active in Jewish civic and philanthropic organizations.<ref name="NYT-Joel">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/06/24/classified/paid-notice-deaths-gross-joel.html |title=Paid Notice: Deaths  GROSS, JOEL |work=[[New York Times]] |date=June 24, 2001 |access-date=February 2, 2026}}</ref> Terry Gross (née Stavisky) was born in New York City to Polish immigrants who had also moved to the United States as teenagers.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> Benedict Gross had two siblings, Ruth Gross Picker and [[Avrum Gross]].<ref name="NYT-Joel"/> [[Al Gross (politician)|Al Gross]] was his nephew.<ref name="NJGlobe">{{cite news |url=https://newjerseyglobe.com/congress/surging-alaska-u-s-senate-candidate-has-new-jersey-ties/ |title=Surging Alaska U.S. Senate candidate has New Jersey ties |first=David |last=Wildstein |work=New Jersey Globe |date=October 16, 2020 |access-date=February 2, 2026}}</ref>

Gross and his family moved to [[Santa Monica, California]], at the age of 5, before returning to New Jersey during second grade.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> He attended [[West Orange High School (New Jersey)|West Orange High School]], but transferred out after his freshman year. Gross graduated from The [[Pingry School]], a leading independent school in New Jersey, in 1967 as the valedictorian.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming">{{cite web |last=Kirby |first=Rob |url=https://celebratio.org/Gross_BH/article/1096/ |title=Benedict H. Gross: Becoming a mathematician |website=[[Celebratio Mathematica]] |date=2023 |access-date=December 4, 2024}}</ref>

He initially studied physics at [[Harvard University]], deterred from mathematics because he thought that his classmates were better prepared than he was, but switched to mathematics in his sophomore year after enjoying the [[Math 55]] course that was taught by [[Andrew M. Gleason]].<ref name="Harvard-Gazette-Obit"/> In 1971, he graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] from Harvard University.<ref name="Harvard-Gazette-Obit"/>

Gross studied music in Africa and Asia, and then moved to [[Oxford University]] as a [[Marshall Scholar]] where he studied history, sociology, and mathematics.<ref name="Harvard-Gazette-Obit"/> He received an M.Sc. from Oxford University in 1974, and then returned to Harvard, where he received his Ph.D. in mathematics in 1978 under the supervision of [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]].<ref name="cv"/><ref name="mg">{{MathGenealogy|id=12980}}</ref>

===Career===
Gross was an assistant professor at [[Princeton University]] from 1978 to 1982, a [[maître de conférences]] at [[Paris Diderot University|Université de Paris VII]] in 1980, and an associate professor at [[Brown University]] from 1982 to 1985.<ref name="cv"/> Gross became a tenured professor at Harvard University in 1985 and became the George Vasmer Leverett Professor at Harvard University in 1988.<ref name="cv"/> He served as Dean of Undergraduate Education from 2002 to 2003 and as the Dean of [[Harvard College]] from 2003 to 2007.<ref>{{Multiref2
| 1 = "[http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2003/4/8/gross-officially-named-dean-of-the/ Gross Officially Named Dean of the College]", ''[[Harvard Crimson]]'', April 8, 2003
| 2 = "[http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2003/5/16/gross-stretches-to-prepare-for-new/ Gross Stretches to Prepare for New Roles]", ''[[Harvard Crimson]]'', May 16, 2003
| 3 = "[http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2007/6/29/with-goals-accomplished-gross-leaves-overhauled/ With Goals Accomplished, Gross Leaves Overhauled College: His efforts were to 'improve the undergraduate experience,' dean says]", ''[[Harvard Crimson]]'', June 29, 2007
| 4 = "[http://www.thecrimson.com/article/2007/9/21/exit-gross-the-magic-of-gross/ Exit Gross]", ''[[Harvard Crimson]]'', September 21, 2007
}}</ref> He retired from Harvard University as a professor emeritus and joined the [[University of California, San Diego]], as a professor in 2016.<ref name="Harvard-Obit"/><ref name="Scripps">{{cite web |url=https://www.scripps.edu/news-and-events/press-room/2018/20181009-benedict-gross-board.html |title=Noted mathematician Benedict Gross joins Scripps Research Board of Directors |date=October 9, 2018 |access-date=January 27, 2026}}</ref>

He was the mathematical consultant for the 1980 film [[It's My Turn (film)|''It's My Turn'']] containing the scene<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=etbcKWEKnvg  |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211222/etbcKWEKnvg |archive-date=December 22, 2021 |url-status=live|title=It's My Turn (1980) Snake Lemma|website=[[YouTube]] |date=January 12, 2009 }}{{cbignore}}</ref> in which actress [[Jill Clayburgh]], portraying a mathematics professor, impeccably proves the [[snake lemma]].<ref>{{cite web| url=https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0343328/| title=Benedict Gross – Miscellaneous Crew| publisher=IMDb.com}}</ref><ref name="Gross Lights Camera">{{cite web | title=Lights, Camera and Algebraic Topology | website=thecrimson.com | date=October 23, 2003 | url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2003/10/23/lights-camera-and-algebraic-topology-imagine/ | access-date=December 31, 2023}}</ref> Gross was a member of the Board of Trustees of the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] from 2012 to 2017<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ias.edu/press-releases/benedict-h-gross-appointed-institute-advanced-study-board-trustees |title=Benedict H. Gross Appointed to Institute for Advanced Study Board of Trustee |publisher=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |date=June 11, 2012 |access-date=January 27, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/documents/publications/G18-30220_AnnualReport.pdf |title=Report for the Academic Year 2016–2017 |publisher=[[Institute for Advanced Study]] |access-date=January 27, 2026}}</ref> and the executive committee of the [[International Mathematical Union]] from 2015 to 2019.<ref name="CV-celebratio">{{cite web |url=https://celebratio.org/Gross_BH/article/1056/ |title=Benedict Gross CV |website=[[Celebratio Mathematica]] |date=2023 |access-date=January 27, 2026}}</ref> He joined the Board of Directors of [[Scripps Research]] in 2018.<ref name="Scripps"/>

==Research==
Gross's work spanned topics in number theory, [[algebraic geometry]], [[modular form]]s, and [[group representation]]s.<ref name="Harvard-Obit"/><ref name="MacArthur">{{cite web |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/class-of-1986/benedict-h-gross |website=[[MacArthur Foundation]] |title=Benedict H. Gross |date=January 1, 2005 |access-date=January 30, 2026}}</ref> His work with [[Don Zagier]] on the [[Gross–Zagier formula]] in 1986 has been influential in modern [[number theory]].<ref name="Harvard-Crimson-Obit"/> It describes the [[Néron–Tate height|height]] of Heegner points in terms of a derivative of the [[L-function]] of elliptic curves<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gross|first1=Benedict H.|author1-link=Benedict Gross|last2=Zagier|first2=Don B.|author2-link=Don Zagier|doi=10.1007/BF01388809|mr=0833192|title=Heegner points and derivatives of L-series|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]|volume=84|year=1986|issue=2|pages=225–320|bibcode=1986InMat..84..225G|s2cid=125716869 }}</ref> and led to breakthroughs on the [[class number problem]] of [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]].<ref name="Harvard-Crimson-Obit"/><ref name="MacArthur"/>

==Personal life and death==
Gross first met his wife [[Jill P. Mesirov]] at a party hosted by [[Robert Langlands]].<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> They married in 1982 and had two sons.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/>

He was diagnosed with [[testicular cancer]] when he was an undergraduate at Harvard University, a likely effect of his mother having been prescribed [[diethylstilbestrol]] during pregnancy to prevent [[miscarriage]].<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> He received radiation therapy to prevent recurrence and had several major abdominal surgeries to deal with issues caused by this radiation over his lifetime.<ref name="Celebratio-becoming"/> Gross died on December 19, 2025, at the age of 75, after a long illness.<ref>{{cite web|title=In Memoriam: Benedict Gross|date=January 27, 2026|publisher=UC San Diego|url=https://math.ucsd.edu/news-events/news/memoriam-benedict-gross|access-date=January 30, 2026|quote=We are deeply saddened to announce the passing of our colleague Benedict (“Dick”) Gross on December 19, 2025.}}</ref><ref name="Harvard-Obit">{{cite web |url=https://www.math.harvard.edu/in-memory-of-professor-emeritus-benedict-gross/ |title=In Memory of Professor Benedict Gross |website=[[Harvard University]] |date=January 16, 2026 |access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref><ref name="Harvard-Crimson-Obit">{{cite news |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2026/1/26/benedict-gross-obituary/ |title=Former College Dean Benedict H. Gross Remembered as 'One of the Kindest People in All of Academia' |work=[[The Harvard Crimson]] |first1=Sebastian B. |last1=Connolly |first2=Summer E. |last2=Rose |date=January 26, 2026 |access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref><ref name="Harvard-Gazette-Obit">{{cite news |url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/newsplus/dick-gross-number-theorist-and-former-college-dean-dies-at-75/ |title=Dick Gross, number theorist and former College dean, dies at 75 |work=The Harvard Gazette |first1=Kermit |last1=Pattison |date=January 23, 2026 |access-date=January 26, 2026}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Gross received a [[MacArthur Fellows Program|MacArthur Fellowship]] in 1986.<ref name="MacArthur"/><ref name="Harvard-Obit"/> Gross, Zagier, and [[Dorian M. Goldfeld]] won the [[Cole Prize]] of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in 1987 for their work on the Gross–Zagier formula and the Gauss class number problem.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/prizes-awards/ams-prizes/cole-prize-number-theory Frank Nelson Cole Prize in Number Theory], AMS, retrieved April 21, 2010.</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Gross | first1=Benedict H. | last2=Zagier | first2=Don B. | title=Heegner points and derivatives ofL-series | journal=Inventiones Mathematicae | volume=84 | issue=2 | date=1986 | issn=0020-9910 | doi=10.1007/BF01388809 | pages=225–320 | bibcode=1986InMat..84..225G | url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01388809 | access-date=January 17, 2026| url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 2012, he became a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved January 19, 2013.</ref>

He was elected as a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1992<ref>[http://www.amacad.org/members/class_section.pdf List of Active Members by Classes] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050506154511/http://www.amacad.org/members/class_section.pdf |date=May 6, 2005 }}, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], retrieved April 21, 2010.</ref> and as a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2004.<ref>[http://www.scienceblog.com/community/older/2004/8/20047575.shtml National Academies news: 72 new members chosen by academy] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303174451/http://www3.scienceblog.com/community/older/2004/8/20047575.shtml |date=March 3, 2016 }}, The National Academies, April 2004, retrieved April 21, 2010.</ref> He was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://amphilsoc.org/members/electedApril2017|title=American Philosophical Society: Newly Elected – April 2017|access-date=June 13, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170915195158/https://amphilsoc.org/members/electedApril2017|archive-date=September 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref>
